[[:db/retract 17592186188931 :question/answer-fields 17592186187632] {:db/id 17592186188279 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-838322c6-867e-5a73-a18d-bbf81bd1218b" "question-b72abcb6-85da-5c4d-a8eb-72ce20ae6b72"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186188931 :question/problem "Let $T:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ be a linear transformation whose standard matrix is $T.$ Which of the following statements are true?

- If $\text{Im}(T)={[x,y,z]^{T}\,:\,3x+2y-z=0}$ then $\text{nullity}(T)=1$
- If ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are two different solutions to $Tx=[1,-2,1]^{T}$ then $T$ is invertible
- If ${v}_{1},$ ${v}_{2},$ and ${v}_{3}$ are the columns of $T$ and ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}+2{v}_{2}$, then $\text{Ker}(T)={0}$" :question/worked-solution "Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{3}$ into ${R}^{3},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Solving $3x+2y-z=0$ for $z,$ we get $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 3x+2y\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are two different solutions to $Tx=[1,-2,1]^{T},$ then 

$$
T{v}_{1}=T{v}_{2}\,⟹\,T({v}_{1}-{v}_{2})=0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}-{v}_{2}$ is a non-zero vector. This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Null}(T)\ne {0}$ and, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ can't be invertible.

- Statement III is false. If the columns of $T$ are such that ${v}_{3}={v}_{1}+2{v}_{2},$ then the set of vectors ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly dependent and therefore $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Col}(T)\ne {R}^{3}.$ Now, according to the matrix invertible theorem, we obtain that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1a41ad32-7f22-5720-8aeb-d6772bd219f3"] :db/ensure  $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T) & =3-\text{nullity}(T) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $Tx=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ has more than one solution, there are ${u}_{1},{u}_{2}\in {R}^{3}$ such that  ${u}_{1}\ne {u}_{2}$ and 

$$
T({u}_{1})=T({u}_{2})=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

This means, $T$ is not a bijection and according to the invertible matrix theorem, $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=1.$ So, $T$ is not a bijection or, which is the same, $T$ is not invertible.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b752c3d9-0b1a-5d80-8a37-82a98660d651"] :db/ensure  $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=3 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=3.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Solving $3x+2y-z=0$ for $z,$ we get $z=3x+2y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ 3x+2y\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+y{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{rank}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =3-2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are two different solutions to $Tx=[1,-2,1]^{T},$ then 

$$
T{v}_{1}=T{v}_{2}\,⟹\,T({v}_{1}-{v}_{2})=0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}-{v}_{2}$ is a non-zero vector. This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Null}(T)\ne {0}$ and, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ can't be invertible.

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=5 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=5.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $\text{Im}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ and the set ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}}$ is linearly independent, we get that $\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=4.$

- Statement II is false. According to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =5-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =5-4 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(T)\ne 5$ (or since $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0$), the linear transformation $T$ cannot be a bijection according to the invertible matrix theorem.

transformations** states the following:

*If $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a linear transformation, then* $$\textrm{dim(Im}(\mathbf{T})) + \textrm{dim(Ker}(\mathbf{T})) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),$$ *or equivalently,* $$\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T}) + \textrm{nullity}(\mathbf{T}) = n.$$

For example, suppose that $\mathbf{T}:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^3$ is a linear transformation such that $$\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\{ [ x, y, z ]^T \, : \, y+2z=0\}.$$

Let's use the rank-nullity theorem to compute $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})$ and $\text{nullity}(\mathbf{T}).$

First, solving $y+2z=0$ for $y,$ we get $y = -2z.$ Therefore, any vector from $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})$ can be written as $$\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ -2z \\ z\end{aligned}]=x{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}$$

This means that $\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{T})=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2\}.$ And since $\mathbf v_1$ and $\mathbf v_2$ are linearly independent, we have $\textrm{rank}(\mathbf{T})=2.$

Finally, using the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain $$\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T) & =3-\text{rank}(T) \\ & =3-2 \\ & =1.\end{aligned}$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "9c4215af-a9cf-5a1a-aabc-40c5395f2df4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4379 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9e0c933b-d880-5bfa-804a-944d21dae8a3" :step/math-academy-id 26840 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189066}} {:db/id 17592186189094 :step/content {:db/id 17592186188287 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186188222 :question/id #uuid "91885df0-9f1d-5c18-acf1-70259cf7f4d9" :question/math-academy-id "e-9987"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9a9a16cc-d807-5015-ba40-b4a15fe3a0db" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186188930} {:db/id 17592186188988} {:db/id 17592186365093} {:db/id 17592186365100} {:db/id 17592186366447} {:db/id 17592186366454}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Rank or Nullity of a Linear Transformation Given a Description of the Image or Kernel"} :step/id #uuid "6735a644-2990-5e5c-b639-afb52f0b4d15" :step/math-academy-id 37613 :step/next {:db/id 17592186189083}}] :activity/title "The Rank-Nullity Theorem in Terms of Linear Transformations" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186188454} {:db/id 17592186189084 :step/content {:db/id 17592186189371 :tutorial/content "The **rank-nullity theorem in terms of linear transformations** states the following:
